name: Atok
line: The highest farm we buy from. Cold nights slow the cherry down, and the cup comes out bright and floral.
story: Atok sits among pine and cloud in the Cordillera, where vegetable terraces give way to coffee under alnus trees. The cherries are picked ripe, pulped the same day and washed clean, then dried on raised beds for about two weeks.

name: Apo
line: Grown on the slopes of the country's tallest mountain and dried whole in the cherry, so the fruit stays in the cup.
story: On the Davao side of Mount Apo, volcanic soil and steady rain grow dense, sweet cherries. They are sorted by hand and dried whole for three to four weeks, turned many times a day, before the dried fruit is hulled away.

name: Kulaman
line: Robusta treated like a specialty coffee: picked ripe, washed and roasted with care. Thick, sweet and built for espresso.
story: The Kulaman plateau grows more coffee than anywhere else in the country, most of it robusta. Ours comes from growers who pick only red cherries and wash them, which takes away the rubbery edge robusta is known for and leaves chocolate and nuts.

name: Amadeo
line: The rare one. Excelsa is tart and fruity even at a darker roast, and tastes like no other coffee on the shelf.
story: Amadeo calls itself the coffee capital of the Philippines, and its tall old excelsa trees are part of the reason. The teardrop beans are dried in the cherry, then roasted a little darker to round off their sharp, tamarind-like tang.

name: Lipa
line: Kapeng barako, the strong coffee of Batangas. Big beans, a dark roast, and an aroma you can smell from the next room.
story: Liberica has grown around Lipa since the 1700s, on trees tall enough to need a ladder. The beans are the largest of the four species. Roasted dark, they give a heavy, smoky cup with a ripe-jackfruit sweetness that Batangueños drink black.
